key_cases.case_name: Kaci May v. Dorchester School District Two
key_cases.citation: Op. No. 6053 (S.C. Ct. App. filed May 29, 2024) (App. Case No. 2020-001352)
key_cases.court: Court of Appeals of South Carolina
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed the denial of an injunction, holding S.C. Code § 63-7-920(C) authorizes DSS to interview children at school without a warrant and outside the parents' presence during a mandated investigation, and that the interviews here were reasonable in inception and scope under the Fourth Amendment.
key_cases.relevance: Kaci May is the leading South Carolina decision on interviews, parental consent and the Fourth Amendment during a CPS assessment.
key_cases.quote: we find § 63-7-920(C) expressly authorizes DSS to interview children at school without a warrant when conducting an investigation mandated by § 63-7-920(A)(1)

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The Fourth Circuit affirmed summary judgment for the county, holding the social worker's and deputies' consented entry into the home was reasonable and that medical examinations of the children did not violate the plaintiff's Fourth Amendment rights.
key_cases.relevance: Wildauer is the controlling circuit statement of how consent and reasonableness operate when CPS enters a home to assess a report.
key_cases.quote: investigative home visits by social workers are not subject to the same scrutiny as searches in the criminal context

key_cases.case_name: Renn ex rel. Renn v. Garrison
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The Fourth Circuit vacated the denial of qualified immunity, holding the social services defendants acted within the authority state statute gave them to investigate reported neglect and that their conduct stayed inside the clearly established boundaries of the family privacy right.
key_cases.relevance: Renn is the Fourth Circuit's substantive statement of the family privacy standard that governs when a caseworker's decision to open and continue an assessment becomes a constitutional intrusion rather than permitted monitoring.
key_cases.quote: we find as well that their actions were reasonable under the circumstances in relation to the boundaries of the family privacy right that had been clearly established

key_cases.case_name: Vosburg v. Department of Social Services
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The Fourth Circuit affirmed summary judgment, holding state social workers are absolutely immune from § 1983 liability for the decision to prepare and file a removal petition, while expressly declining to extend that absolute immunity to their investigative conduct.
key_cases.relevance: Vosburg is the Fourth Circuit decision establishing that a caseworker's investigative conduct, unlike the decision to petition, carries at most a good-faith qualified immunity — the proposition Wildauer later relies on.
key_cases.quote: We emphasize, however, that our grant of absolute immunity applies only to those activities of social workers that could be deemed prosecutorial.
